In the ordered computational basis $(|0\rangle,|1\rangle)$ of [[def-qc-qubit-and-bloch-representation]], define the identity and Pauli endomorphisms of $Q_2$ by
$$I=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.$$

The displayed sign in $Y$ fixes all later orientation and rotation conventions.

For the matrices $X,Y,Z$ of [[def-qc-pauli-matrices]], each is self-adjoint and unitary, and $X^2=Y^2=Z^2=I$. Distinct Pauli matrices anticommute. For $j,k\in\{x,y,z\}$,
$$\sigma_j\sigma_k=\delta_{jk}I+i\sum_{\ell\in\{x,y,z\}}\epsilon_{jk\ell}\sigma_\ell,\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\sigma_j\sigma_k)=2\delta_{jk}.$$
Here $\sigma_x=X,\sigma_y=Y,\sigma_z=Z$, $\delta_{jk}=1$ when $j=k$ and $0$ otherwise, and $\epsilon$ is the alternating symbol with $\epsilon_{xyz}=1$. Also $\operatorname{tr}(I)=2$ and $\operatorname{tr}(\sigma_j)=0$.

In the computational basis $(|0\rangle,|1\rangle)$, use $X,Y,Z$ from [[def-qc-pauli-matrices]] and define
$$H:=\frac{X+Z}{\sqrt2}=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad S:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&i\end{pmatrix},\qquad T:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix}.$$
The phases displayed in these matrices are exact; they are not identified modulo a scalar when the matrices are later placed under a control.

For real $\theta$ and a real unit vector $\mathbf n=(n_x,n_y,n_z)$, define the axis rotation
$$R_{\mathbf n}(\theta):=\exp\!\left(-\frac{i\theta}{2}\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\right),\qquad R_z(\theta):=R_{(0,0,1)}(\theta).$$
Here $\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}$ and $\|\mathbf n\|_2$ have the meanings fixed in [[def-qc-bloch-coordinate-map]]. For a bounded endomorphism $B$ of $Q_2$, the notation $\exp(B)$ means the operator-norm series $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}B^k/k!$ of [[lem-exponential-series-of-a-bounded-operator]] at scalar parameter $1$. Its convergence applies here because $Q_2$ is finite-dimensional and complete and every linear endomorphism of $Q_2$ is bounded ([[cor-finite-dimensional-normed-spaces-are-banach]], [[cor-linear-maps-with-finite-dimensional-domain-are-bounded]]).

The unitary identities for the fixed matrices are verified below. The following theorem proves the closed form and unitarity of each $R_{\mathbf n}(\theta)$.

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

Let $(T_k:H_k\to K_k)_{k<n}$ and $(S_k:K_k\to L_k)_{k<n}$ be finite ordered
families of linear maps between finite-dimensional complex inner-product
spaces. Then

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}S_k\right)\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)=\bigotimes_{k<n}(S_kT_k),\qquad \bigotimes_{k<n}I_{H_k}=I_{\otimes_{k<n}H_k},\qquad \left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)^*=\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k^*.$$

In the first formula, $S_kT_k$ means $S_k\circ T_k$. Here $I_{H_k}$ denotes
the identity map $x\mapsto x$. All adjoints use the
repository pairing, linear in the first argument. The empty tensor-map
identity is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on $\mathbb C$.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

derivations.claim: On one factor, $Z^{z_j}X^{x'_j}=(-1)^{z_jx'_j}X^{x'_j}Z^{z_j}$, since the factors commute unless both exponents are $1$, when $ZX=-XZ$ by [F1]. Multiplying these identities over the ordered factors gives $Z^zX^{x'}=(-1)^pX^{x'}Z^z$, where $p$ is the integer representative $0$ or $1$ of $z\cdot x'\in\mathbb F_2$.

Substituting that reordering into $i^{k+k'}X^xZ^zX^{x'}Z^{z'}$ gives $i^{k+k'+2p}X^{x+x'}Z^{z+z'}$, which is exactly the stated product formula; all binary exponents add modulo $2$, while the phase exponent adds modulo $4$.
The formula proves closure. $P(0,0,0)=I$ is an identity, and associativity is inherited from matrix multiplication, so $\mathcal P_n$ is a group once inverses are supplied below.

Taking the adjoint reverses the order and conjugates $i^k$: $(i^kX^xZ^z)^*=i^{-k}Z^zX^x=i^{-k}(-1)^pX^xZ^z=P(2p-k,x,z)$, where $p$ represents $x\cdot z$. The product formula then gives $P^*P=PP^*=I$, so this adjoint is the inverse and completes the group proof.

Scalar operators $i^kI$ commute with every matrix and belong to $\mathcal P_n$. Conversely, if $P(k,x,z)$ commutes with every $X_j$, the product law forces $z_j=0$ for each $j$; commuting with every $Z_j$ forces $x_j=0$ for each $j$. Thus every central element is scalar and the center is exactly $Z_n$.

A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

derivations.claim: The identity conjugates $\mathcal P_n$ to itself. If $U,V\in\mathcal C_n$, then $(UV)\mathcal P_n(UV)^*=U(V\mathcal P_nV^*)U^*=U\mathcal P_nU^*=\mathcal P_n$, so $UV\in\mathcal C_n$.

In the ordered computational basis $(|0\rangle,|1\rangle)$ of [[def-qc-qubit-and-bloch-representation]], define the identity and Pauli endomorphisms of $Q_2$ by
$$I=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.$$

The displayed sign in $Y$ fixes all later orientation and rotation conventions.

For the matrices $X,Y,Z$ of [[def-qc-pauli-matrices]], each is self-adjoint and unitary, and $X^2=Y^2=Z^2=I$. Distinct Pauli matrices anticommute. For $j,k\in\{x,y,z\}$,
$$\sigma_j\sigma_k=\delta_{jk}I+i\sum_{\ell\in\{x,y,z\}}\epsilon_{jk\ell}\sigma_\ell,\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\sigma_j\sigma_k)=2\delta_{jk}.$$
Here $\sigma_x=X,\sigma_y=Y,\sigma_z=Z$, $\delta_{jk}=1$ when $j=k$ and $0$ otherwise, and $\epsilon$ is the alternating symbol with $\epsilon_{xyz}=1$. Also $\operatorname{tr}(I)=2$ and $\operatorname{tr}(\sigma_j)=0$.

Let $C=\mathbb C^2$ be a control qubit with ordered orthonormal basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$, let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, and let $U:H\to H$ be unitary. On the control-first register $C\otimes H$, define

$$C(U):=\begin{pmatrix}I_H&0\\0&U\end{pmatrix}.$$

Thus $C(U)(|0\rangle\otimes v)=|0\rangle\otimes v$ and $C(U)(|1\rangle\otimes v)=|1\rangle\otimes Uv$. **Controlled access** means that the chosen operation model explicitly grants a call to this block operator. An ordinary call to a black-box $U$ does not silently grant a controlled call, and no query or gate cost is assigned unless the model states it.

In the ordered two-qubit basis $|00\rangle,|01\rangle,|10\rangle,|11\rangle$, the controlled-NOT with first wire control and second wire target is

$$\operatorname{CNOT}_{1\to2}|a,t\rangle=|a,t\mathbin{\oplus}a\rangle,\qquad a,t\in\{0,1\}.$$

Equivalently, it is the control block $C(X)=\operatorname{diag}(I,X)$ of [[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]], where $X$ is the Pauli bit-flip matrix. The wire order is part of the definition.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

Let $(T_k:H_k\to K_k)_{k<n}$ and $(S_k:K_k\to L_k)_{k<n}$ be finite ordered
families of linear maps between finite-dimensional complex inner-product
spaces. Then

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}S_k\right)\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)=\bigotimes_{k<n}(S_kT_k),\qquad \bigotimes_{k<n}I_{H_k}=I_{\otimes_{k<n}H_k},\qquad \left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)^*=\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k^*.$$

derivations.claim: For control $c=1$ and target $t=2$, the controlled-X definition [F3,F4] gives $C|y_1,\ldots,y_n\rangle=|y_1,\ldots,y_t+y_c,\ldots,y_n\rangle$. Applying this rule twice gives $C^2=I$; it permutes the ordered orthonormal basis, so $C=C^*$. On a basis vector, in $C X_c C$ the right CNOT first changes $y_t$ to $y_t+y_c$, the middle $X_c$ changes $y_c$ to $y_c+1$, and the left CNOT changes the target to $y_t+y_c+(y_c+1)=y_t+1$. Thus $C X_c C=X_cX_t$. In $C X_t C$, the right CNOT changes the target to $y_t+y_c$, the middle $X_t$ toggles it, and the left CNOT toggles it back by $y_c$, leaving $y_t+1$; hence $C X_t C=X_t$. The middle $Z_c$ contributes $(-1)^{y_c}$ and the two CNOTs restore the bits, giving $C Z_c C=Z_c$. The middle $Z_t$ contributes $(-1)^{y_t+y_c}$, giving $C Z_t C=Z_cZ_t$.

For arbitrary distinct wires $c,t\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, assign source positions $0,1$ to $c-1,t-1$. This partial assignment is injective; list its remaining source and target positions in increasing order and match them in order to extend it to a permutation $\sigma$. By [F6], $P_\sigma$ moves those factors into the first two positions and permutes an orthonormal basis bijectively, so $P_\sigma$ is unitary. The operator $P_\sigma^{-1}(C_{1\to2}\otimes I_{\rm remaining})P_\sigma$ therefore has the stated basis action, and its Pauli conjugation rules are the first-two-wire rules of step 1.1 with local wire names $1,2$ replaced by $c,t$.

Write $P(k,x,z)$ as its ordered product of all $X$-factor maps followed by all $Z$-factor maps. Conjugation preserves this product order. Using step 2.1, the images of the $X$ factors combine to $X_c^{x_c}X_t^{x_t+x_c}$ with all other $X$ exponents unchanged; the images of the $Z$ factors combine to $Z_c^{z_c+z_t}Z_t^{z_t}$ with all other $Z$ exponents unchanged. Tensor-map composition in [F5] justifies these factorwise products, and no $X$ factor is moved past a $Z$ factor. Thus no scalar is introduced, $k$ is unchanged, and the stated binary updates follow.

Let $Z_n$ be the scalar center of $\mathcal P_n$. Define $P\sim Q$ when $P^{-1}Q\in Z_n$, and let $Q_n$ be the set of equivalence classes $[P]=PZ_n$. The proposed coset product is $[P][Q]=[PQ]$. The quotient theorem verifies this product is well-defined and proves that the assignment

$$\lambda:Q_n\longrightarrow V_n:=\mathbb F_2^n\oplus\mathbb F_2^n,\qquad [P(k,x,z)]\longmapsto(x,z)$$

is a group isomorphism to the additive group of $V_n$. A binary label deliberately forgets the scalar phase.

For every prime $p$, the operations of addition and multiplication on
$\mathbb Z/p$ make it a field ([[def-field]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

A subset $B \subseteq V$ is a **basis of $V$** when

- **(B1)** $B$ is linearly independent ([[def-linear-independence]]), and
- **(B2)** $B$ spans $V$, that is $\operatorname{span}(B) = V$
  ([[def-linear-combination-and-span]], which is where the words *spans* and
  *spanning set* are fixed; they are not redefined here).

**The empty set is a basis of the zero space, and of nothing else.**
$\varnothing$ is linearly independent ([[def-linear-independence]]) and
$\operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
([[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]]), so $\varnothing$ is a basis of
$V$ exactly when $V = \{0_V\}$. This is the case $n = 0$ from which every
induction on this page starts, and it is a genuine case rather than a convention.

### Ordered bases

An **ordered basis of $V$** is a finite list $v : n \to V$, with $n \in
\mathbb{N}$ and $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ the von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), such that $v$ is
injective ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]) and its image $v[n]$ is a
basis of $V$.

By claim 6 of [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]], a list is linearly
independent exactly when it is injective with linearly independent image, so an
ordered basis is equally described as a **linearly independent list $v : n \to V$
with $\operatorname{span}(v[n]) = V$**: the injectivity does not have to be
imposed separately. The empty list is the ordered basis of the zero space.

An ordered basis is a list, so it carries an order; a basis is a set, so it does
not. Reordering an ordered basis gives a different ordered basis with the same
image, and the coordinates of
[[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]] are attached to the
list, not to the set.

### Bases of a linear subspace

Let $U$ be a linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]), which is itself a
vector space over $F$, with the addition, the zero vector and the scalar
multiplication of $V$ restricted to $U$. For $A \subseteq U$ the two readings of
"$A$ is a basis" — computed inside $U$, or computed inside $V$ — agree, so the
phrase needs no disambiguation below.

- **Independence agrees.** The finite sums $\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i a_i$ of a list
  $a : n \to U$ are given by the same recursion in $U$ as in $V$
  ([[def-monoid-finite-product]]), the base value $0_V$ and the operation $+$
  being literally those of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). So a list into $U$ has
  the same sums whichever space it is read in, and the vanishing condition of
  [[def-linear-independence]] is the same condition in both.
- **The span agrees.** A subset of $U$ is a linear subspace of $U$ exactly when it
  is a linear subspace of $V$, conditions (W1), (W2), (W3) being the same
  conditions in either reading. Now $\operatorname{span}_V(A) \subseteq U$, since
  $U$ is a linear subspace of $V$ containing $A$ and the span is contained in
  every such subspace; so $\operatorname{span}_V(A)$ is a linear subspace of $U$
  containing $A$, whence $\operatorname{span}_U(A) \subseteq \operatorname{span}_V(A)$.
  Conversely $\operatorname{span}_U(A)$ is a linear subspace of $V$ containing
  $A$, whence $\operatorname{span}_V(A) \subseteq \operatorname{span}_U(A)$. The
  two are therefore equal, and we write $\operatorname{span}(A)$ for both.

Consequently $A \subseteq U$ is a basis of the vector space $U$ if and only if
$A$ is linearly independent as a subset of $V$ and $\operatorname{span}(A) = U$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

$V$ is **finite-dimensional over $F$** when it has a **finite** basis
([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-countable]]): some basis $B$ of $V$ satisfies
$B \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]).

For $n\ge0$ and a binary word $x=(x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1})\in\{0,1\}^n$, define its
**big-endian index**

$$\operatorname{enc}_n(x):=\sum_{k<n}x_k\,2^{\,n-1-k}.$$

$\{0,1\}^0$ consists only of the empty word $()$, and the empty sum gives
$\operatorname{enc}_0(())=0$. In an ordered $n$-qubit
computational basis, the word $x$ occupies the slot numbered

$n$ bit positions therefore induces a permutation of the corresponding
computational basis.

In the ordered computational basis $(|0\rangle,|1\rangle)$ of [[def-qc-qubit-and-bloch-representation]], define the identity and Pauli endomorphisms of $Q_2$ by
$$I=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.$$

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

spaces. Then

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}S_k\right)\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)=\bigotimes_{k<n}(S_kT_k),\qquad \bigotimes_{k<n}I_{H_k}=I_{\otimes_{k<n}H_k},\qquad \left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)^*=\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k^*.$$

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

A subset $B \subseteq V$ is a **basis of $V$** when

- **(B1)** $B$ is linearly independent ([[def-linear-independence]]), and
- **(B2)** $B$ spans $V$, that is $\operatorname{span}(B) = V$
  ([[def-linear-combination-and-span]], which is where the words *spans* and
  *spanning set* are fixed; they are not redefined here).

**The empty set is a basis of the zero space, and of nothing else.**
$\varnothing$ is linearly independent ([[def-linear-independence]]) and
$\operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
([[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]]), so $\varnothing$ is a basis of
$V$ exactly when $V = \{0_V\}$. This is the case $n = 0$ from which every
induction on this page starts, and it is a genuine case rather than a convention.

### Ordered bases

An **ordered basis of $V$** is a finite list $v : n \to V$, with $n \in
\mathbb{N}$ and $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ the von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), such that $v$ is
injective ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]) and its image $v[n]$ is a
basis of $V$.

By claim 6 of [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]], a list is linearly
independent exactly when it is injective with linearly independent image, so an
ordered basis is equally described as a **linearly independent list $v : n \to V$
with $\operatorname{span}(v[n]) = V$**: the injectivity does not have to be
imposed separately. The empty list is the ordered basis of the zero space.

An ordered basis is a list, so it carries an order; a basis is a set, so it does
not. Reordering an ordered basis gives a different ordered basis with the same
image, and the coordinates of
[[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]] are attached to the
list, not to the set.

### Bases of a linear subspace

Let $U$ be a linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]), which is itself a
vector space over $F$, with the addition, the zero vector and the scalar
multiplication of $V$ restricted to $U$. For $A \subseteq U$ the two readings of
"$A$ is a basis" — computed inside $U$, or computed inside $V$ — agree, so the
phrase needs no disambiguation below.

- **Independence agrees.** The finite sums $\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i a_i$ of a list
  $a : n \to U$ are given by the same recursion in $U$ as in $V$
  ([[def-monoid-finite-product]]), the base value $0_V$ and the operation $+$
  being literally those of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). So a list into $U$ has
  the same sums whichever space it is read in, and the vanishing condition of
  [[def-linear-independence]] is the same condition in both.
- **The span agrees.** A subset of $U$ is a linear subspace of $U$ exactly when it
  is a linear subspace of $V$, conditions (W1), (W2), (W3) being the same
  conditions in either reading. Now $\operatorname{span}_V(A) \subseteq U$, since
  $U$ is a linear subspace of $V$ containing $A$ and the span is contained in
  every such subspace; so $\operatorname{span}_V(A)$ is a linear subspace of $U$
  containing $A$, whence $\operatorname{span}_U(A) \subseteq \operatorname{span}_V(A)$.
  Conversely $\operatorname{span}_U(A)$ is a linear subspace of $V$ containing
  $A$, whence $\operatorname{span}_V(A) \subseteq \operatorname{span}_U(A)$. The
  two are therefore equal, and we write $\operatorname{span}(A)$ for both.

Consequently $A \subseteq U$ is a basis of the vector space $U$ if and only if
$A$ is linearly independent as a subset of $V$ and $\operatorname{span}(A) = U$.

Applying both sides to $|0^n\rangle$ gives nonzero multiples of $|x\rangle$ and $|x'\rangle$; distinct bit strings index distinct basis vectors by [F2], so $x=x'$. Applying the operators to $|e_j\rangle$ gives the common output basis vector $|e_j+x\rangle$ with coefficients $i^k(-1)^{z_j}$ and $\lambda i^{k'}(-1)^{z'_j}$; their equality and the preceding phase equality imply $z_j=z'_j$ for every $j$. citations.quote: For a Hadamard gate $H_j$ on factor $j$, conjugation swaps the binary coordinates $x_j,z_j$ and changes the phase exactly by $2x_jz_j$ modulo $4$. In particular $HXH=Z$, $HZH=X$, and $HYH=-Y$.

For a phase gate $S_j=\operatorname{diag}(1,i)$ on factor $j$, the binary update is $(x_j,z_j)\mapsto(x_j,z_j+x_j)$ and the phase update is $k\mapsto k+x_j$ modulo $4$. In particular $SXS^*=Y$ and $SZS^*=Z$.

Let $n\ge2$ and let distinct $c,t\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ be control and target indices. For CNOT $C_{c\to t}$ acting on $y\in\mathbb F_2^n$ by toggling coordinate $t$ by $y_c$, conjugation sends

$$P(k,x,z)\longmapsto P(k,x',z'),\qquad x'_t=x_t+x_c,\quad z'_c=z_c+z_t,$$

with all other coordinates unchanged and additions in $\mathbb F_2$. In particular, $X_c\mapsto X_cX_t$, $Z_c\mapsto Z_c$, $X_t\mapsto X_t$, and $Z_t\mapsto Z_cZ_t$; the phase coordinate $k$ is unchanged in the fixed $X^xZ^z$ order.
For $P(k,x,z)=i^kX^xZ^z\in\mathcal P_n$, the operator is Hermitian exactly when $k\equiv x\cdot z\pmod 2$. In that case $P(k,x,z)^2=I$.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

On $V_n=\mathbb F_2^n\oplus\mathbb F_2^n$, with coordinate order $(x,z)$, define

$$\omega((x,z),(x',z')):=x\cdot z'+z\cdot x'.$$

This is a nondegenerate alternating bilinear form over $\mathbb F_2$; $V_n$ has dimension $2n$. In characteristic two, alternating also implies symmetry.

Work with actual unitary matrices, not equivalence classes modulo global phase. The $n$-qubit **Clifford normalizer** is

$$\mathcal C_n:=\{U\text{ unitary on }\mathcal H_n:U\mathcal P_nU^*=\mathcal P_n\}.$$

It is a group under matrix multiplication. Every scalar unitary $\lambda I$ with $|\lambda|=1$ belongs to $\mathcal C_n$ and has the same conjugation action as $I$; the chosen convention retains these distinct matrices.

derivations.claim: Each listed gate and its inverse normalizes $\mathcal P_n$ by its exact Pauli action. On binary labels, $H_j$ preserves $\omega$ because swapping $x_j,z_j$ in both arguments leaves $x_jz'_j+z_jx'_j$ unchanged by [F6]. For $S_j$, the local pairing becomes $x_j(z'_j+x'_j)+(z_j+x_j)x'_j=x_jz'_j+z_jx'_j+2x_jx'_j$, equal to the old value in $\mathbb F_2$; its inverse has the same label action. For CNOT $c\to t$, write $a=(x,z)$ and $b=(u,w)$, with $w$ the $z$-part of $b$. The affected contribution after the updates in [F3] is $x_c(w_c+w_t)+(x_t+x_c)w_t+(z_c+z_t)u_c+z_t(u_t+u_c)$. The added terms $x_cw_t$ and $z_tu_c$ each occur twice and cancel, leaving the original pairing. By [F5], wire swaps permute the paired coordinate summands and preserve the form. Hadamard and swap are involutions, CNOT is self-inverse, and $S_j^*$ is the inverse of $S_j$; hence each binary gate map is invertible. Thus every finite gate word $G$ has an invertible symplectic map $M_G$, and its unitary lies in $\mathcal C_n$ by [F7].

Let $h\in\{0,1\}$ be the representative of $x\cdot z\in\mathbb F_2$, so $P(h,x,z)$ is Hermitian by [F4]. Choose a wire $p$ on which $v$ is nonzero and swap it to wire $1$. On each supported wire, the local factor is proportional to $X$, $Y$, or $Z$. Apply no gate to an $X$ factor, $H$ to a $Z$ factor, and $S^*$ to a $Y$ factor; [F1] and [F2] send each local binary label to $X$, while their phase updates compute the accumulated scalar exactly modulo $4$. The resulting binary label is the nonempty product of $X$ on the support of $v$.

For each other supported wire $j$, apply CNOT $1\to j$. By [F3], it sends $X_1X_j$ to $X_1$, so the finite list removes all $X_j$ labels while retaining $X_1$; then apply $H_1$ to change $X_1$ to $Z_1$. This constructs a circuit $C$ with $CP(h,x,z)C^*=\pm Z_1$: conjugation preserves Hermiticity, so the phase of an image with label $(0,e_1)$ is $0$ or $2$ modulo $4$. For $D=C^*$, the induced symplectic map sends the label $z_1=(0,e_1)$ of $Z_1$ to $v$.

The binary action of $S_1$ is $\tau_{z_1}$ by [F2], since [F6] gives $\omega((x,z),(0,e_1))=x_1$. Therefore $DS_1D^*$ acts by $M_D\tau_{z_1}M_D^{-1}=\tau_v$: for any $w$, symplecticity of $M_D$ gives $M_D(M_D^{-1}w+\omega(M_D^{-1}w,z_1)z_1)=w+\omega(w,v)v$. The circuit lies in $\mathcal C_n$ by step 1.1.

Each gate formula in [F1]–[F3] gives the exact image phase in $\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z$ as well as the binary label; [F5] gives the exact no-change phase for swaps. Induction on the finite gate list for $DS_1D^*$ therefore computes each generator-image phase by repeated application of those formulas, without replacing it by its binary parity.

citations.quote:
On $V_n=\mathbb F_2^n\oplus\mathbb F_2^n$, with coordinate order $(x,z)$, define

$$\omega((x,z),(x',z')):=x\cdot z'+z\cdot x'.$$

This is a nondegenerate alternating bilinear form over $\mathbb F_2$; $V_n$ has dimension $2n$. In characteristic two, alternating also implies symmetry.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

A subset $B \subseteq V$ is a **basis of $V$** when

- **(B1)** $B$ is linearly independent ([[def-linear-independence]]), and
- **(B2)** $B$ spans $V$, that is $\operatorname{span}(B) = V$
  ([[def-linear-combination-and-span]], which is where the words *spans* and
  *spanning set* are fixed; they are not redefined here).

**The empty set is a basis of the zero space, and of nothing else.**
$\varnothing$ is linearly independent ([[def-linear-independence]]) and
$\operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
([[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]]), so $\varnothing$ is a basis of
$V$ exactly when $V = \{0_V\}$. This is the case $n = 0$ from which every
induction on this page starts, and it is a genuine case rather than a convention.

### Ordered bases

An **ordered basis of $V$** is a finite list $v : n \to V$, with $n \in
\mathbb{N}$ and $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ the von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), such that $v$ is
injective ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]) and its image $v[n]$ is a
basis of $V$.

By claim 6 of [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]], a list is linearly
independent exactly when it is injective with linearly independent image, so an
ordered basis is equally described as a **linearly independent list $v : n \to V$
with $\operatorname{span}(v[n]) = V$**: the injectivity does not have to be
imposed separately. The empty list is the ordered basis of the zero space.

An ordered basis is a list, so it carries an order; a basis is a set, so it does
not. Reordering an ordered basis gives a different ordered basis with the same
image, and the coordinates of
[[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]] are attached to the
list, not to the set.

### Bases of a linear subspace

Let $U$ be a linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]), which is itself a
vector space over $F$, with the addition, the zero vector and the scalar
multiplication of $V$ restricted to $U$. For $A \subseteq U$ the two readings of
"$A$ is a basis" — computed inside $U$, or computed inside $V$ — agree, so the
phrase needs no disambiguation below.

- **Independence agrees.** The finite sums $\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i a_i$ of a list
  $a : n \to U$ are given by the same recursion in $U$ as in $V$
  ([[def-monoid-finite-product]]), the base value $0_V$ and the operation $+$
  being literally those of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). So a list into $U$ has
  the same sums whichever space it is read in, and the vanishing condition of
  [[def-linear-independence]] is the same condition in both.
- **The span agrees.** A subset of $U$ is a linear subspace of $U$ exactly when it
  is a linear subspace of $V$, conditions (W1), (W2), (W3) being the same
  conditions in either reading. Now $\operatorname{span}_V(A) \subseteq U$, since
  $U$ is a linear subspace of $V$ containing $A$ and the span is contained in
  every such subspace; so $\operatorname{span}_V(A)$ is a linear subspace of $U$
  containing $A$, whence $\operatorname{span}_U(A) \subseteq \operatorname{span}_V(A)$.
  Conversely $\operatorname{span}_U(A)$ is a linear subspace of $V$ containing
  $A$, whence $\operatorname{span}_V(A) \subseteq \operatorname{span}_U(A)$. The
  two are therefore equal, and we write $\operatorname{span}(A)$ for both.

Consequently $A \subseteq U$ is a basis of the vector space $U$ if and only if
$A$ is linearly independent as a subset of $V$ and $\operatorname{span}(A) = U$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

$V$ is **finite-dimensional over $F$** when it has a **finite** basis
([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-countable]]): some basis $B$ of $V$ satisfies
$B \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]).

For such a $V$, the **dimension of $V$ over $F$**, written $\dim_F V$, is that
$n$:

$$\dim_F V \;:=\; \text{the unique } n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } V \text{ has a basis } B \text{ with } B \approx n .$$

**This is well defined.** Existence of such an $n$ is the hypothesis, together
with the fact that a finite set is equinumerous with exactly one natural number
([[lem-pigeonhole]], claim 3). Uniqueness is
[[thm-any-two-finite-bases-have-the-same-size]]: two bases of $V$ with $n$ and
with $m$ elements force $n = m$. That theorem is therefore a **prerequisite** of
this definition, not a later justification of it, and it is listed in `deps`.

$V$ is **infinite-dimensional over $F$** when it is not finite-dimensional over
$F$, that is, when $V$ has **no** finite basis. No number is attached to such a
space here: the symbol $\dim_F V$ is defined only in the finite-dimensional case,
and the expression $\dim_F V = \infty$ is not used.

**The zero space.** $\varnothing$ is a basis of $\{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-basis]]) and $\varnothing \approx 0$, so $\{0_V\}$ is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F \{0_V\} = 0$. Conversely a space of dimension $0$
has a basis $B \approx 0$, that is $B = \varnothing$, and then
$V = \operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces over the same field $F$. A function
$T:V\to W$ is **linear** when

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or
**linear transformation**.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

The set of **natural numbers** is the **smallest inductive set**
([[def-inductive-set]]),

$$\mathbb{N} = \omega := \bigcap\,\{\, I : I \text{ is inductive} \,\},$$

which exists and is itself inductive by [[lem-omega-smallest-inductive]] (the
Axiom of Infinity, [[def-axiom-of-infinity]], supplies one inductive set to
intersect within, and Separation, [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]], makes the
intersection a set). On $\mathbb{N}$ we take

$$0 := \varnothing, \qquad \sigma(n) := n \cup \{n\},$$

the distinguished element and the successor function. Thus
$0 = \varnothing$, $1 = \{0\}$, $2 = \{0, 1\}$, $3 = \{0, 1, 2\}$, and in general
$n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ is the set of its predecessors.

derivations.claim: For $s\in\{0,1,2,3\}$, the standard coordinate vectors form a basis of $\mathbb F_2^s$ by coordinate expansion and coordinatewise independence, so $\dim\mathbb F_2^s=s$. Let $d\in\{2,3\}$ and let $U$ be a proper subspace of $\mathbb F_2^d$. Since $U$ is finite, choose a linearly independent subset $B\subseteq U$ maximal under inclusion; maximality makes it span $U$, since any vector outside its span could be adjoined while preserving independence. If $r=|B|$, its $2^r$ binary coefficient lists give distinct vectors by independence and exhaust $U$ by spanning, so $|U|=2^r$. But $|\mathbb F_2^d|=2^d$ and $U$ is proper, hence $r<d$. Enumerate $B=(q_1,\ldots,q_r)$ and define $A_B:\mathbb F_2^d\to\mathbb F_2^r$ by $A_B(\alpha)=(\alpha\cdot q_1,\ldots,\alpha\cdot q_r)$. Each coordinate dot product is linear in $\alpha$, so $A_B$ is linear [F4]. Its domain and codomain have dimensions $d$ and $r$ by the coordinate-basis calculation. Its image is a finite subspace; a maximal independent subset spans it as above, and its $2^{\operatorname{rank}A_B}$ distinct binary combinations lie among the $2^r$ vectors of $\mathbb F_2^r$, so its rank is at most $r$. Thus rank-nullity [F2] gives $\dim\ker A_B=d-\operatorname{rank}A_B\ge d-r>0$. For nonzero $\alpha\in\ker A_B$, every basis vector $q_i$ satisfies $\alpha\cdot q_i=0$, so linearity and spanning give $\alpha\cdot u=0$ for every $u\in U$. The functional $u\mapsto\alpha\cdot u$ is nonzero because its value on a coordinate vector with nonzero corresponding coordinate of $\alpha$ is $1$.

Alternation and bilinearity imply $0=\omega(u+w,u+w)=\omega(u,w)+\omega(w,u)$ for all $u,w$; since subtraction equals addition in $\mathbb F_2$, $\omega$ is symmetric. For $v=0$, $\tau_v$ is the identity. For any $v$, alternation gives $\omega(v,v)=0$, so applying $\tau_v$ twice adds $\omega(w,v)v$ twice and returns $w$. For $u,w\in V$, bilinearity gives $$\omega(\tau_vu,\tau_vw)=\omega(u,w)+\omega(w,v)\omega(u,v)+\omega(u,v)\omega(v,w).$$ Symmetry from the first sentence makes the last two terms the same product, which sums to zero in $\mathbb F_2$; therefore $\tau_v$ preserves $\omega$.
At $n=0$, $\dim V=0$ implies $V=\{0\}$ by [F3]. Its identity is the only symplectic map and is the empty composition of transvections.

These maps act transitively on nonzero vectors. If $a=b$, no map is needed. If $\omega(a,b)=1$, then $v=a+b$ satisfies $\omega(a,v)=1$, hence $\tau_v(a)=b$. If $a\ne b$ and $\omega(a,b)=0$, then $a,b$ are independent over $\mathbb F_2$. Their pairing functionals are independent: a relation $r\omega(a,\cdot)+s\omega(b,\cdot)=0$ gives $\omega(ra+sb,w)=0$ for every $w$, so nondegeneracy gives $ra+sb=0$, and independence gives $r=s=0$. The map $L(w)=(\omega(a,w),\omega(b,w))$ is linear by bilinearity. If its image were proper, step 1.1 would give a nonzero $\alpha\in\mathbb F_2^2$ with $\alpha\cdot L(w)=0$ for every $w$. This would make a nontrivial linear combination of the pairing functionals zero, a contradiction. Thus $L$ is onto; choose $c$ with both pairings $1$. By symmetry from step 1.2, $\omega(c,b)=1$, so $\tau_{a+c}(a)=c$ and $\tau_{c+b}(c)=b$.

Fix $e,f$ with $\omega(e,f)=1$. If $y$ and $f$ both pair to $1$ with $e$, then transvections fixing $e$ send $y$ to $f$ as follows. If $y=f$, use the identity. If $\omega(y,f)=1$, the center $y+f$ lies in $e^\perp$ and $\tau_{y+f}(y)=f$. If $y\ne f$ and $\omega(y,f)=0$, the vectors $e,y,f$ are independent: pairing a relation $r e+s y+t f=0$ with $e$ gives $s=t$ by symmetry from step 1.2; if $s=t=1$, then $y+f=r e$, which would give either $y=f$ or $\omega(y,f)=\omega(f+r e,f)=r=1$, both impossible. Their pairing functionals are independent because a relation among them is the pairing with the corresponding linear combination of $e,y,f$, which nondegeneracy forces to be zero. The map $L(w)=(\omega(e,w),\omega(y,w),\omega(f,w))$ is linear by bilinearity. If its image were proper, step 1.1 would give a nonzero $\alpha\in\mathbb F_2^3$ annihilating every value of $L$, contradicting independence of the three pairing functionals. Hence $L$ is onto; choose $c$ with all three values $1$. The centers $y+c$ and $c+f$ lie in $e^\perp$, and $\tau_{c+f}\tau_{y+c}(y)=f$; both transvections fix $e$.

Assume $n\ge1$ and the result for dimension $2(n-1)$. For the application $V=V_n$, the nondegenerate alternating form hypotheses hold by [F1]; the following argument is for any such $V$. Since $\dim V=2n>0$, choose $e\ne0$; nondegeneracy gives $f$ with $\omega(e,f)=1$. Let $T_0$ be symplectic. By step 2.1, choose a finite product $A$ of transvections with $A(T_0e)=e$, and set $T_1=AT_0$. The vector $y=T_1f$ satisfies $\omega(e,y)=1$, so step 3.1 gives a finite product $B$ of transvections fixing $e$ and sending $y$ to $f$. Thus $G=BT_1$ is symplectic and fixes both $e$ and $f$. Let $W=\{w:\omega(w,e)=\omega(w,f)=0\}$. Bilinearity makes $W$ a subspace and $\Phi:V\to\mathbb F_2^2$, $\Phi(u)=(\omega(u,f),\omega(u,e))$, linear by [F4]; it is onto because $\Phi(e)=(1,0)$ and $\Phi(f)=(0,1)$, and its kernel is $W$. Step 1.1 gives $\dim\mathbb F_2^2=2$, so rank-nullity [F2] yields $\dim W=\dim V-2=2(n-1)$. For any $u$, bilinearity and $\omega(e,f)=1$ show that $w=u+\omega(u,f)e+\omega(u,e)f$ lies in $W$, so every $u$ is a sum of an element of $E=\{r e+s f:r,s\in\mathbb F_2\}$ and an element of $W$; the intersection is zero since pairing $r e+s f\in W$ with $f$ and $e$ gives $r=s=0$. Thus $V=E\oplus W$. The restriction of $\omega$ to $W$ is nondegenerate: a vector in its radical is orthogonal to $W,e,f$, hence to all of $V$, and is zero. Since $G$ and $G^{-1}$ fix $e,f$ and preserve $\omega$, both map $W$ to itself, so $G|_W$ is an invertible symplectic map. By the induction hypothesis, $G|_W$ is a finite product of transvections centered in $W$. Those same transvections fix $e,f$ in $V$ and agree with $G$ on $W$, so their product is $G$ on $V=E\oplus W$. If $p\in\{0,1\}$ represents $x\cdot z\in\mathbb F_2$, then $P(k,x,z)^*=P(2p-k,x,z)=P(k,x,z)^{-1}$, and its center is $Z_n=\{i^k I:k\in\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z\}$.

On $V_n=\mathbb F_2^n\oplus\mathbb F_2^n$, with coordinate order $(x,z)$, define

$$\omega((x,z),(x',z')):=x\cdot z'+z\cdot x'.$$
